_provenance.written_in_session: From 2026-09-30, from public sources only (listed under each place); no API batch (AGENTS.md).
_provenance.rules: Plain English, no praise words, figures only where a listed source publishes them, never 'official boundary' (spec §18). Exactly one key fact 'Established YYYY (27 CFR 9.N)', as TTB lists it. Descriptions of 2-4 sentences, at most 700 characters. At most 8 grapes; the 1-3 signature grapes are PRINCIPAL and the rest ACCESSORY. At least two sources per place, one of them the CFR section or the Federal Register final rule. share_pct is left out.

article.description: An AVA of about 38,000 acres on the Mayacamas slopes northeast of Santa Rosa, between the Russian River Valley, Knights Valley and Sonoma Valley. It is named after the Fountain Grove colony that Thomas Lake Harris founded in 1875, whose winery Kanaye Nagasawa later ran. About 500 acres are planted.
article.climate: Warm, Region II on the Winkler scale: warmer than the Russian River Valley but more marine-influenced than Alexander Valley and northern Napa.
article.soils: Rolling hills with soils from Sonoma Volcanics and Franciscan Formation bedrock.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon, with Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Zinfandel and Syrah.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines led by Cabernet Sauvignon, and dry whites.

article.description: A low, rolling AVA at the north shore of San Pablo Bay, spanning the southern ends of Napa and Sonoma counties. It was the first AVA defined by its climate rather than by geography, and it is known for Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling wine. The name, "the rams", dates from Mexican land grants of the 1830s, and the land was sheep ranches, dairies and hay fields before vines took over in the 1970s.
article.climate: Cool and windy: marine air and fog come straight off San Pablo Bay, summer days rarely pass 80 °F, the difference between day and night is small, and rainfall, at up to about 24 inches, is the lowest in Napa Valley.
article.soils: Shallow, dense clay soils, not very fertile, over a hard claypan that keeps roots near the surface and holds yields down; loams and hillside alluvium in the north.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay above all, with Merlot, Syrah and some Cabernet Sauvignon.
article.wine_styles: Dry Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and sparkling wine made from both.

article.description: California's first AVA, a valley about 30 miles long between the Mayacamas Mountains to the west and the Vaca Range to the east, in Napa County. Fifteen smaller AVAs lie within it, from Calistoga at the northern end to Coombsville and Oak Knoll District near the city of Napa, and Los Carneros and Wild Horse Valley overlap its southern edge. It is known above all for Cabernet Sauvignon.
article.climate: A dry Mediterranean climate: warm, rainless summers and mild, wet winters. Fog and wind from San Pablo Bay cool the southern end, and the valley grows warmer toward Calistoga in the north; the mountain AVAs above the fog line see fewer swings between day and night.
article.soils: Very varied over short distances: gravelly and sandy alluvial fans and river deposits on the valley floor, volcanic soils from ash and lava on the eastern side and in the hills, and marine sedimentary soils on the western slopes.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon above all, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and the other Bordeaux varieties; Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc for whites; Zinfandel and Pinot Noir in smaller amounts.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, mostly Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux-style blends, dry whites from Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc, and sparkling wine from the cooler south.

article.description: A mountain AVA on the western slopes of the Vaca Range, east of the Stags Leap District and the city of Napa, named after the 2,663-foot Atlas Peak. Most of the area lies above 1,400 feet, above much of the valley fog. Wines labelled Atlas Peak must also carry the Napa Valley name.
article.climate: A cool mountain climate with less fog than the valley floor: summer days are about 10 to 15 °F cooler than on the valley floor and rarely pass 90 °F, and the difference between day and night is wide.
article.soils: Volcanic soils, often red and basaltic, shallow and quick-draining, so vineyards usually need irrigation.
article.grape_varieties: Mainly Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, above all Cabernet Sauvignon, and dry Chardonnay.

article.description: The northernmost AVA on the Napa Valley floor, around the town of Calistoga below Mount St. Helena, closed in by mountains on three sides. It is the warmest part of the valley floor, and its soils are largely volcanic. Wines labelled Calistoga must also carry the Napa Valley name.
article.climate: Warm to hot days, with summer peaks above 100 °F, and cold nights that can fall to the low 40s °F as air drains down from the surrounding mountains; one of the widest day-to-night swings in Napa Valley.
article.soils: Mostly volcanic: rocky and stony loams on the hillsides, gravelly and cobbly loams on the alluvial fans, and heavier clay and silt toward the centre of the valley.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon first, with Zinfandel, Petite Sirah, Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, from Cabernet Sauvignon to Zinfandel and Petite Sirah, and some Sauvignon Blanc.

article.description: A long, narrow valley in the Vaca Range in the northeast of Napa County, higher and set apart from the main Napa Valley. It has more vineyards than wineries, and it is named after Joseph Ballinger Chiles, who received a land grant here in 1841. Wines labelled Chiles Valley must also carry the Napa Valley name.
article.climate: Warm summer days, typically in the mid-80s °F, and cool nights below 50 °F because of the elevation; winters and springs are colder than on the Napa Valley floor, and harvest comes later.
article.soils: Mostly of marine origin: fertile alluvial silty clay on the valley floor and clay loams and stony clays on the hillsides, with some volcanic outcrops.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Zinfandel, with some Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, mainly Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Zinfandel.

article.description: A horseshoe of hills directly east of the city of Napa, at the foot of the Vaca Range, near the southern end of Napa Valley. It is mostly vineyards, with few wineries, and was known first for Chardonnay and Pinot Noir before Cabernet Sauvignon took over. Wines labelled Coombsville must also carry the Napa Valley name.
article.climate: Cool for Napa Valley: San Pablo Bay is close, marine fog comes in most days of the growing season, and in the hottest months average highs can run up to 10 °F below those of other Napa AVAs.
article.soils: Largely volcanic: rhyolitic tuff and old lava flows with plenty of rock, gravel and ash on the uplands, and alluvial soils in the lower parts.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay and Merlot, with Pinot Noir and Syrah.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, above all Cabernet Sauvignon, and dry Chardonnay.

article.description: A hillside AVA of about 4,000 acres on the western face of the Vaca Range, east of St. Helena and south of Howell Mountain. It covers slopes between 400 and 1,400 feet, with no flat ground, and about 230 acres of vineyard in some 30 commercial vineyards when it was established in 2024. It was Napa Valley's first new AVA in 13 years.
article.climate: The slopes face west and southwest and receive more sun than north- or east-facing ground; below 1,400 feet they keep a maritime influence, and the final rule notes that ground above and below the band is more prone to frost.
article.soils: Thin, well-drained volcanic soils, with volcanic ash on slopes of 15 to 40 percent.
article.grape_varieties: Mainly Cabernet Sauvignon, planted on the hillside vineyards.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, chiefly Cabernet Sauvignon.

article.description: A mountain AVA in the Mayacamas range just south of Calistoga, at the northwest end of Napa Valley. Its name comes from shards of volcanic glass in the soil. Jacob Schram planted vines here in 1862. Wines labelled Diamond Mountain District must also carry the Napa Valley name.
article.climate: Mostly above the fog line: summer days rarely pass 90 °F and run 10 to 15 °F cooler than on the valley floor, with smaller swings between day and night; Diamond Creek's drainage brings cool air.
article.soils: Reddish, fine-grained volcanic soils, sometimes gritty, weathered from uplifted volcanic and sedimentary rock; porous and quick-draining.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon dominates, with Cabernet Franc, Merlot and Petit Verdot.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, chiefly Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux-style blends.

article.description: A plateau in the Vaca Range above St. Helena, around the village of Angwin, and the first AVA established inside Napa Valley. Its southern edge was set at 1,400 feet, where the fog tops out, so its vineyards lie above the valley's fog. Wines labelled Howell Mountain must also carry the Napa Valley name.
article.climate: Above the fog line on the eastern side of the valley: warmer and drier than much of Napa Valley, with more hours of sun and little marine influence.
article.soils: Shallow volcanic soils of low fertility that drain freely, from iron-rich red soils to white compressed volcanic ash (tuff).
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon above all, with Merlot, Zinfandel and Cabernet Franc; a little Chardonnay and Viognier.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, mostly Cabernet Sauvignon and Zinfandel, and a few whites.

article.description: A mountain AVA on the eastern slopes of the Mayacamas range, northwest of the city of Napa, along the line between Napa and Sonoma. It is one of the larger Napa sub-AVAs but among the least planted, because the ground is steep and wooded. It is named after the 1850s pastor Peter Veeder. Wines labelled Mt. Veeder must also carry the Napa Valley name.
article.climate: Cool for Napa: summer days run 10 to 15 °F below the valley floor, with mid-summer highs around 85 °F, and most vineyards sit above the fog line.
article.soils: Shallow, acidic, sandy and sandy-loam soils of marine sedimentary origin, an old seabed with Franciscan mélange beneath and rare volcanic pockets; well drained and low in fertility.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon above all, with Zinfandel, Merlot, Chardonnay and Syrah.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, mainly Cabernet Sauvignon and Zinfandel, and dry Chardonnay.

article.description: A flat stretch of the valley floor at the southern end of central Napa Valley, just north of the city of Napa. Joseph Osborne planted vinifera vines here in 1851. The legal name ends in "of Napa Valley", so it already carries the valley's name.
article.climate: Cool and even: daily fog from San Pablo Bay and afternoon breezes give one of the valley's coolest sub-AVAs and a long growing season; mid-summer highs reach about 92 °F and nights fall to about 50 °F.
article.soils: River-laid soils in the centre, gravelly alluvial fans on the west side below Mt. Veeder, and silty clay loams toward the river in the south and east.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay and Merlot, with Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines from Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, and dry whites from Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling.

article.description: A valley-floor AVA in the middle of Napa Valley, running from the Mayacamas foothills on the west to the Vaca foothills on the east, between Yountville and Rutherford. About three quarters of its vineyard is Cabernet Sauvignon. Wines labelled Oakville must also carry the Napa Valley name.
article.climate: Moderately warm, with summer days commonly in the mid-90s °F; evening and early-morning fog keeps acidity in the grapes, and the eastern side gets more afternoon sun.
article.soils: Gravelly, sedimentary alluvial loams on the western side and heavier volcanic soils on the eastern side; fairly deep and well drained.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon above all, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, mainly Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux-style blends, and dry Sauvignon Blanc.

article.description: A valley-floor AVA at the widest point of Napa Valley, between Oakville and St. Helena, from the Mayacamas benchland on the west to the Vaca foothills on the east. Georges de Latour's Beaulieu winery made its name here after Prohibition. Wines labelled Rutherford must also carry the Napa Valley name.
article.climate: Moderately warm, with summer peaks in the mid-90s °F, early-morning fog and a wide difference between day and night; the western bench is cooled by afternoon marine wind.
article.soils: Sedimentary, gravelly and sandy alluvial soils on the western benchland and moderately deep volcanic soils on the eastern side; locals speak of "Rutherford dust" for the fine-grained tannin of the bench wines.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon dominates, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, mostly Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux-style blends, and dry Sauvignon Blanc.

article.description: A mountain AVA on the eastern slopes of the Mayacamas range directly west of St. Helena, with small vineyards cut into forest on steep, mostly east-facing ground. Charles Lemme is the first documented grape grower here, in 1874. Wines labelled Spring Mountain District must also carry the Napa Valley name.
article.climate: Cool to moderate depending on height and aspect: warmer nights and cooler days than the valley floor, and the coolest, wettest of the Napa sub-AVAs.
article.soils: Mostly sedimentary: weathered sandstone and shale, loamy and friable, well drained and low in fertility, over Franciscan mélange in the south; volcanic soils toward the north end.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon first, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petite Sirah, Chardonnay and Riesling.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, mainly Cabernet Sauvignon, and some dry Chardonnay and Riesling.

article.description: An hourglass-shaped AVA around the town of St. Helena, taking in the narrowest part of Napa Valley between Rutherford and Calistoga. Charles Krug founded his winery here in 1861. Wines labelled St. Helena must also carry the Napa Valley name.
article.climate: One of the warmer parts of the Napa Valley floor, at times hotter than Calistoga, with rainfall of about 40 inches a year.
article.soils: Alluvial fans from both sides of the valley: gravelly loams on the western side and volcanic soils washed down from the eastern hills.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon first, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Zinfandel, Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, mostly Cabernet Sauvignon, and dry whites.

article.description: A small AVA on the east side of Napa Valley, about six miles north of the city of Napa, some three miles long and one mile wide between the Stags Leap palisades and the Napa River. In the 1976 Paris tasting a Stag's Leap Wine Cellars Cabernet Sauvignon placed first among the reds. Wines labelled Stags Leap District must also carry the Napa Valley name.
article.climate: Moderately warm, with mid-summer highs in the mid-90s °F and up to 100 °F; the palisades funnel cool afternoon air from San Pablo Bay through the district and cool the nights.
article.soils: Volcanic gravelly loams on the valley floor and rocky hillsides, of low to moderate fertility over hard clay subsoils.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon dominates, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot and some Sauvignon Blanc.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, chiefly Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux-style blends.

article.description: A valley-floor AVA around the town of Yountville and its low hills, in the southern part of Napa Valley between Oak Knoll District and Oakville. It is named after George C. Yount, who planted the first vines here in the 1840s. Wines labelled Yountville must also carry the Napa Valley name.

article.soils: Mainly gravelly silt loams of sedimentary origin and rocky alluvial soils of moderate fertility.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, with Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines from Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, and dry whites.

article.description: A large umbrella AVA over northern Sonoma County that takes in Alexander Valley, Dry Creek Valley, Knights Valley, Russian River Valley and its sub-AVAs, from valley floors to mountain peaks. It was petitioned by E. & J. Gallo so that its Sonoma wines from vineyards in different valleys could carry one appellation, and few labels use it today.
article.climate: Varied: cool and foggy toward the Russian River Valley and the coast, warmer in the inland valleys of Alexander and Knights Valley.
article.soils: Varied, from river gravels and alluvium on the valley floors to volcanic and sedimentary soils in the hills.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay and Zinfandel, with Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir and Merlot.
article.wine_styles: Dry red and white wines, from Cabernet Sauvignon and Zinfandel to Chardonnay.

article.description: The valley of the upper Russian River in Sonoma County, from the Mendocino County line southeast to Healdsburg, with the Mayacamas range to the east. It is Sonoma County's largest planted AVA, known for Cabernet Sauvignon since the 1960s and 1970s. It is named after the pioneer Cyrus Alexander; the Italian Swiss Colony was founded at Asti in the 1880s.
article.climate: Warm days with heat spikes, tempered by cool marine air from the Pacific that brings cool evenings.
article.soils: Alluvial soils laid down by the meandering Russian River over gravel deposits, with hillside soils on the benches and slopes.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon first, with Merlot and other Bordeaux varieties, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and old-vine Zinfandel.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, mostly Cabernet Sauvignon, and dry whites from Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc.

article.description: A narrow valley about 16 miles long and 2 miles wide northwest of Healdsburg, running from the Russian River up to Lake Sonoma. It is known above all for Zinfandel, including old vines that survived Prohibition when growers switched to prunes, and for Sauvignon Blanc. Over 70 wineries, mostly family-owned, work here.
article.climate: In between the cooler Russian River Valley and warmer Alexander Valley: fog tempers the valley in the mornings without dominating it.
article.soils: Very rocky, free-draining soils, planted on hillsides, benches and the valley floor.
article.grape_varieties: Zinfandel first, with Sauvignon Blanc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Petite Sirah and the Rhône varieties Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, above all Zinfandel, and dry Sauvignon Blanc.

article.description: A warm, high valley in eastern Sonoma County below Mount St. Helena, between Alexander Valley and Napa's Calistoga, reached by Highway 128. It is named after Thomas B. Knight, and it has stayed rural: cattle and vineyards, few wineries. Cabernet Sauvignon and the other Bordeaux varieties lead.
article.climate: Warm and inland, cut off from most of the coastal fog, with cooler air at night coming down from the surrounding hills.
article.soils: Soils of the valley floor and of the lower slopes of Mount St. Helena, an old volcano that towers over the valley.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon and other Bordeaux varieties lead, with Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Syrah.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, mainly Cabernet Sauvignon, and dry Sauvignon Blanc.

article.description: A cool AVA at the centre of Sonoma County, on the lower Russian River and the Santa Rosa Plain, from Healdsburg south toward Sebastopol and Santa Rosa. It does not follow the river all the way to the sea. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are its main grapes, then Zinfandel. Most of it also lies inside the Sonoma Coast AVA, which overlaps it.
article.climate: Warm days tempered by Pacific fog that lingers in the hills west of Sebastopol into the late afternoon; temperatures can drop 35 to 40 °F from day to night, and the growing season runs long.
article.soils: Varied; the fine-grained Goldridge sandy loam, well drained and moderate in vigour, dominates its western Green Valley corner.
article.grape_varieties: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Zinfandel lead by acreage, with Sauvignon Blanc, Syrah, Merlot and Pinot Gris.
article.wine_styles: Dry Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, Zinfandel, and sparkling wine from the cooler western parts.

article.description: A hilly corner of the Russian River Valley east of Windsor, rising to about 1,600 feet toward Knights Valley. The pale soil that gave it its name is not chalk but white volcanic ash. It has more than 1,400 acres of vineyard but only a handful of wineries.
article.climate: Warmer than most of the Russian River Valley, with less fog and steady breezes.
article.soils: White, quartz-rich volcanic tuff (ash) that looks like chalk, with loams on the slopes.
article.grape_varieties: Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc, with Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Cabernet Franc; some Syrah and Zinfandel.
article.wine_styles: Dry whites from Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc, and Bordeaux-variety reds.

article.description: The coolest, foggiest corner of the Russian River Valley, in wooded hills between Sebastopol, Occidental and Forestville, following the watersheds of Green Valley, Atascadero and Purrington creeks. Apple orchards shared the land with vines for decades. It was called Sonoma County Green Valley until 2007, when it was renamed to avoid confusion with Solano County Green Valley.
article.climate: Fog arrives early and stays late: the hills trap it, so days are cool and the range between day and night is narrow; sheltered from much of the wind.
article.soils: Goldridge fine sandy loam dominates: well drained, deep-rooting, and moderately vigorous, with enough clay to hold some moisture in dry years.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, with Syrah a distant third.
article.wine_styles: Dry Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and sparkling wine from both.

article.description: A wind-defined AVA of about 202,500 acres across southern Sonoma County and northern Marin County, from the Pacific to San Pablo Bay. A gap in the coastal hills lets ocean wind and fog flow inland, and the AVA is drawn around that corridor. Pinot Noir is about three quarters of its vineyard.
article.climate: Windy and cool: afternoon wind through low hills of under 600 feet lowers photosynthesis, so grapes hang longer, with smaller berries and thicker skins, and can be picked at lower sugar.
article.soils: Varied soils on low rolling hills; the petition defined the area by its wind rather than its soils.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir about 75% of the vineyard, then Chardonnay and Syrah.
article.wine_styles: Dry Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Syrah, and some sparkling wine.

article.description: A mountain AVA of about 4,600 acres on the ridges northeast of Cloverdale, along Pine Mountain Road, crossing from Sonoma into Mendocino County. Only land above the 1,600-foot contour is included, and about 230 acres are planted, around 80% of them to Cabernet Sauvignon.
article.climate: Often above morning fog: days are cooler and lightly breezy, nights warmer than in the valleys below.
article.soils: Mountain soils among oak woodland, madrone and scrub, with spring-fed ponds between the vineyard blocks.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon about 80% of the vineyard, with Merlot, Malbec and Cabernet Franc.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, mainly Cabernet Sauvignon.

article.description: A ridge-top AVA in northwest Sonoma County, above Dry Creek Valley and overlooking Lake Sonoma. It covers only ground above the 800-foot contour; of some 15,000 acres, about 160 are planted, mostly since 1992. It is known for Zinfandel.
article.climate: Sunny, with less fog than the valleys below: an inversion layer from Lake Sonoma keeps the fog beneath the vineyards.
article.soils: Upland soils on steep ridges; before vines the area was sheep ranches and hunting clubs for about a century.
article.grape_varieties: Zinfandel first, with Cabernet Sauvignon, Petite Sirah and Syrah.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, above all Zinfandel, and some Petite Sirah and Syrah.

article.description: Sonoma County's largest AVA, reaching from the wind-swept Pacific coast in the north to the salt marshes of San Pablo Bay in the south. It holds West Sonoma Coast and Fort Ross-Seaview, and overlaps the Russian River Valley and Los Carneros. Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are its main grapes.
article.climate: Shaped by the Pacific: afternoon fog covers the lower ground while ridge-top vineyards often rise above it, and wind and fog pour in through the Petaluma Gap in the south.
article.soils: Varied: thin, sandy soils over Franciscan rocks on the coastal ridges and heavy adobe clays near San Pablo Bay in the south.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, with Syrah as a runner-up and some Zinfandel.
article.wine_styles: Dry Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and sparkling wine.

article.description: The westernmost strip of Sonoma County, about 141,800 acres of steep coastal ridges along the San Andreas fault, from Annapolis in the north through Fort Ross-Seaview to Freestone and Occidental. It lies within Sonoma Coast and holds all of Fort Ross-Seaview. At establishment it had about 47 commercial vineyards and some 1,028 acres of vines.
article.climate: Marine: days cooler and nights warmer than inland, fewer growing degree days than to the east, and less wind than the Petaluma Gap to the south; many vineyards sit above the fog.
article.soils: Thin, sandy, well-drained soils over hard Franciscan Complex rocks, unlike the Wilson Grove Formation farther east.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, with some Syrah.
article.wine_styles: Dry Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and some Syrah.

article.description: Ridge-top land above Fort Ross State Historic Park, between Jenner and The Sea Ranch, overlooking the Pacific. The AVA covers only ground above the 920-foot contour, so its vineyards sit above the marine layer. Russian settlers planted grapes at Fort Ross in 1817; modern planting began in 1973.
article.climate: Cool and close to the cold Pacific, but above the fog: the ridges get more summer sun than the coast and valleys below.
article.soils: Thin, well-drained soils on steep coastal ridges over Franciscan rocks.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, with some Syrah and Zinfandel.
article.wine_styles: Dry Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from ridge-top vineyards.

article.description: The valley of Sonoma Creek in southeast Sonoma County, between the Mayacamas range and Sonoma Mountain, from Sugarloaf Ridge down to San Pablo Bay, with the town of Sonoma at its heart. Commercial winemaking in California began here in the 1850s, and old Zinfandel plantings date from then. It holds Bennett Valley, Moon Mountain District and Sonoma Mountain.
article.climate: Three zones: mild days and cool bay winds in the flat south near Carneros, warmer around Glen Ellen where Sonoma Mountain holds the heat, and cooler again in the north around Kenwood, where Pacific fog and wind reach.
article.soils: Fertile, loamy soils that hold water on the valley floor, and meagre, rocky, well-drained soils higher up the slopes.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon is now the leading grape, with old-vine Zinfandel, Merlot, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Syrah.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines from Cabernet Sauvignon and Zinfandel, and dry Chardonnay.

article.description: A small upland valley south of Santa Rosa, ringed by Sonoma Mountain, Bennett Peak and Taylor Mountain, on high ground between Sonoma Valley and the Cotati Valley. Isaac DeTurk founded a winery here in 1862; after phylloxera and Prohibition the vines returned in the late 1970s with Matanzas Creek. About 650 acres are planted.
article.climate: Cool: Pacific air and fog reach it through the Petaluma Gap and Crane Canyon on summer afternoons.
article.soils: Clay-like volcanic soils on the valley floor and the surrounding slopes.
article.grape_varieties: Merlot and Chardonnay made its name, with Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Syrah and Sauvignon Blanc.
article.wine_styles: Dry Merlot, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, and some Syrah.

article.description: The western slopes of the Mayacamas range above Sonoma Valley, facing Sonoma Mountain across the valley, from about 200 to 2,200 feet. About 1,500 of its 17,663 acres are planted. It holds the Monte Rosso vineyard, first planted in 1886 and named by Louis M. Martini in 1938. The legal name already includes "Sonoma County".
article.climate: Afternoon sun with crosswinds from the Pacific and San Pablo Bay; the higher vineyards get stronger sun.
article.soils: Rocky, iron-rich volcanic soils and loams.
article.grape_varieties: Zinfandel and Cabernet Sauvignon, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Malbec and some Chardonnay.
article.wine_styles: Dry red wines, mostly Cabernet Sauvignon and old-vine Zinfandel.

article.description: The north and east slopes of Sonoma Mountain above Glen Ellen, in the northwest of Sonoma Valley, between about 400 and 1,200 feet. Its vineyards are scattered among woods and grazing land; Jack London farmed here. About 800 acres are planted.
article.climate: The eastern slopes are sheltered from fog, sunny and warm; the western flank gets cool wind and fog from the Petaluma Gap.
article.soils: Hillside soils on a series of stacked hills dotted with live oak, the vineyards isolated among woods and grazing land.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon on the warm eastern side, Pinot Noir on the western side, with Chardonnay, Syrah, Sauvignon Blanc and Zinfandel.
article.wine_styles: Dry Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinot Noir, and dry Chardonnay.

article.description: A small upland AVA in the hills east of the city of Napa, straddling the line between Napa and Solano counties. Most of it lies above the fog, and its vineyards were first planted in 1881 and replanted from 1978. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are its main grapes.
article.climate: The coolest of the AVAs that reach into Napa Valley, because of its height and San Pablo Bay nearby; summer days rarely pass 90 °F and the difference between day and night is small.
article.soils: Shallow volcanic soils with little water-holding capacity, so irrigation is usually needed.
article.grape_varieties: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, planted from 1978 on.
article.wine_styles: Dry Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from upland vineyards.
